strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: machine learning for high-speed compressible flows with adaptive time-stepping.
Introduces two new supersonic flow datasets (coal dust explosion and circular blast) that could be useful for the community.
Proposes a clear two-phase framework (neural CFL + time-conditioned neural solver) and explores several physically motivated CFL features and timestep conditioning strategies.
Provides extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and supplementary results across multiple neural solver backbones.
weaknesses: No comparison to existing neural PDE solvers or classical adaptive solvers, and no uniform time-stepping baseline to demonstrate the claimed benefits of adaptive time-stepping over fixed-step alternatives.
No wall-clock speedup or accuracy-cost tradeoff evaluation, so the practical significance for accelerating high-speed flow modeling remains unclear.

The proposed timestep conditioning strategies (Euler residuals, Mixture of Experts) yield mixed and inconsistent improvements; in several cases the base conditioning is best or differences are within error bars, weakening the central methodological contribution.

The neural CFL model is trained on ground-truth states and timesteps but deployed autoregressively on predicted states, with no scheduled sampling, robustness analysis, or oracle comparison to isolate timestep prediction errors from solver errors.

Novelty is limited: supervised timestep prediction plus conditioning follows existing work on time-conditioned neural solvers and adaptive/continuous-time PDE learning; the distinction mainly rests on using solver-generated adaptive temporal data.
Evaluation lacks physical metrics such as shock position, pressure, or wave speed errors, and does not test generalization across a wider range of Mach numbers or geometries.
Reproducibility is weakened by a questionable dataset DOI/link and the absence of a code release or detailed data-generation scripts.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: adaptive time-stepping for high-speed compressible flows, where shock waves and sharp gradients make uniform time-stepping impractical.
Proposes a clear two-phase framework, ShockCast, combining a neural CFL model for timestep prediction with a timestep-conditioned neural solver.
Systematically studies several physically motivated neural CFL input variants, including spatial gradients, max pooling, and CFL-inspired features.
Explores multiple timestep conditioning strategies across several neural solver backbones, including U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, and Transolver.
Generates two supersonic flow datasets (coal dust explosion and circular blast), which could be useful to the community if properly released.
Provides substantial appendix material with hyperparameters, extended results, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly establish the value of the proposed framework. There is no comparison to classical adaptive time-stepping, uniform time-stepping neural solvers, or existing adaptive neural PDE methods, so the claimed benefits of temporal adaptivity remain unsupported.

The central motivation is computational savings, yet no wall-clock speedup, solver-step reduction, or cost analysis is reported. Without such evidence, the practical significance of ShockCast is unclear.

Many empirical improvements are marginal and often within error bars. No timestep-conditioning strategy consistently wins across datasets/metrics, weakening the claimed contribution of the proposed conditioning techniques.

Some reported metrics are suspicious or uninformative. For example, the coal dust explosion gas velocity x-component correlation time is exactly 80.00 with zero standard error for every model, suggesting a metric artifact or hidden cap rather than meaningful model behavior.

The autoregressive rollout analysis is incomplete. The neural CFL model is evaluated mainly one-step, but at inference it consumes its own predicted states; error accumulation, distribution shift, and sensitivity to predicted versus ground-truth Δt are not adequately studied.

The novelty is limited. The two-phase idea is natural, and several components—time-conditioned layer norm, spatial-spectral conditioning, Euler residual connections, and MoE—are adapted from prior work. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its conceptual contribution beyond applying these ideas to high-speed flows.

The claim of being the first framework for learning high-speed flows / temporal re-meshing is overbroad and not carefully positioned against related work in adaptive neural PDE solvers, Taylor-expansion methods, and continuous-time models.

Reproducibility is weak. No code release is mentioned, data generation depends on the specialized HyBurn code, and the provided DOI for the datasets appears invalid or at least highly unusual, raising serious concerns about data availability.

Generalization is not demonstrated. Experiments are limited to two coarsened, simplified cases with reduced domains and subsets of field variables; it is unclear whether the method extends to more realistic hypersonic, reactive, or multiphase flows.

Presentation and reporting have issues. Main-text figures are not self-contained, numerical results are mostly relegated to the appendix, and several differences are not shown to be statistically significant.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: neural solvers for high-speed compressible flows where uniform time-stepping is impractical.
Proposes a clear two-phase framework, ShockCast, that couples a neural CFL timestep predictor with a timestep-conditioned neural solver in an autoregressive rollout.

Introduces and systematically studies several timestep-conditioning strategies for neural PDE solvers, including time-conditioned layer norm, spatial-spectral conditioning, Euler residuals, and timestep-conditioned Mixture of Experts.
Develops physically motivated neural CFL input features and architectural choices based on the classical CFL condition, such as spatial gradients, max-pooling, and CFL variables.
Generates and releases two new supersonic flow datasets, coal dust explosion and circular blast, which could be useful for future work on compressible neural solvers.
Provides a broad empirical study across four neural solver backbones and multiple conditioning variants, with evaluation beyond one-step error, including correlation time, mean flow, and TKE.
Includes useful implementation details, hyperparameters, compute usage, and extended results in the appendix, supporting reproducibility to a reasonable degree.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat limited: the framework mostly combines existing ideas such as timestep prediction, time-conditioned neural solvers, neural ODE-inspired residuals, and MoE conditioning, applied to a new domain.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to relevant prior adaptive or continuous-time neural PDE methods (e.g., TANTE, Poseidon, learned interpolators/neural fields, or other adaptive time-stepping neural solvers), making it difficult to judge whether ShockCast advances the state of the art.
No wall-clock runtime, speedup, or cost-accuracy comparison against classical adaptive solvers is reported, despite computational acceleration being a central motivation for the work.

The proposed timestep conditioning strategies are not consistently better than the base models; in several cases improvements are small and error bars overlap, weakening the evidence that the novel conditioning mechanisms are necessary or clearly beneficial.

Long-horizon accuracy is mixed: for the coal dust explosion, correlation time for some fields remains low (e.g., gas velocity y-component), suggesting limited ability to reliably resolve complex multiphase shock-driven dynamics over time.

The neural CFL model is supervised to emulate timesteps from a coarsened version of the data-generation solver rather than learning an error-controlled or stability-aware adaptive policy, which limits the significance and generality of the timestep prediction component.

The scope is relatively narrow: only two 2D simulated datasets and maximum Mach numbers below 3 are considered, so the "high-speed" claim does not cover hypersonic or 3D regimes, and generalization to new conditions or resolutions is not demonstrated.

The claim of being the first framework for learning high-speed flows is stronger than the evidence and positioning provided; related work on adaptive neural time-stepping and compressible flows should be discussed and compared more carefully.
Data/code availability is somewhat unclear: the provided dataset DOI/link appears unusual, and no code repository is mentioned, which may hinder reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: adaptive time-stepping for learned high-speed flow modeling, where uniform time-stepping is often impractical.
Proposes a coherent two-phase framework (neural CFL + timestep-conditioned neural solver) and evaluates it across several neural solver backbones and timestep-conditioning strategies.

Introduces physically motivated input features and architectural choices for neural CFL prediction, including spatial gradients, max pooling, CFL-derived features, and timestep conditioning via time-conditioned layer norm, spatial-spectral conditioning, Euler residuals, and MoE.

Generates three new supersonic-flow datasets (coal dust explosion, circular blast, airfoil shock) and includes additional 3D, long-rollout, and hypersonic extensions, which may be useful to the community.
Evaluation is broad in terms of architectures and settings, with runtime analyses, mass-conservation checks, ablation of neural CFL (oracle vs mean baseline), and long-rollout visualizations.
weaknesses: The paper lacks direct comparisons to prior adaptive/continuous-time neural PDE solvers it discusses (e.g., TANTE, Janny et al., Hagnberger et al., Gupta & Brandstetter, Herde et al.), making the claimed novelty and relative effectiveness difficult to assess.

The main accuracy results compare mostly variants of the authors' own framework rather than strong external baselines such as continuous-time neural solvers, fixed-step neural solvers, or classical adaptive solvers under matched cost/accuracy budgets.

The timestep-conditioning strategies often yield inconsistent or marginal improvements, and MoE conditioning is substantially more expensive without consistently better accuracy, weakening the practical case for the proposed conditioning mechanisms.

Performance on the coal dust explosion dataset is not strong for a central high-speed multiphase case: correlation-time proportions are around 60%, with y-velocity correlation near 20%, suggesting limited long-horizon predictive validity in that setting.

The hypersonic evaluation is relegated to the appendix, uses a modified setup that drops one velocity field, and reports that the more general MGN model failed, so the framework's scalability and robustness in truly hypersonic regimes remain unclear.

The neural CFL model is trained on coarsened timestep targets obtained from saved snapshots rather than the instantaneous CFL timestep, and the implications of this mismatch for the learned timestep policy and for inference-time distribution shift are not fully analyzed.
Reproducibility is partially compromised by missing or malformed links to code/data in the abstract, despite otherwise detailed training and implementation descriptions.

The paper claims to be the first to learn temporal re-meshing with adaptable temporal resolution, but related work on adaptive time-stepping and continuous-time querying is not sufficiently benchmarked to substantiate that positioning.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively under-explored problem: adaptive time-stepping for machine-learning surrogates of high-speed compressible flows.
Proposes a sensible two-phase framework that couples a neural CFL timestep predictor with a timestep-conditioned neural solver.

Introduces and describes several physically motivated neural CFL input features and conditioning strategies, including time-conditioned layer norm, spatial-spectral conditioning, Euler residuals, and MoE-based conditioning.
Generates new supersonic-flow datasets covering multiphase coal dust explosion, circular blast, and airfoil shock cases, with additional 3D spherical and long-horizon circular-blast extensions.

Evaluation spans multiple neural solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver, MGN/DGN), neural CFL ablations, oracle/mean-Delta-t comparisons, feature importance, mass conservation, and runtime analyses.
Provides a detailed appendix with CFD setup, training hyperparameters, architecture descriptions, and qualitative visualizations, which helps clarify implementation.
Shows reasonable performance in some settings, e.g., circular blast correlation time and mass conservation, and reports GPU runtime advantages over classical solvers in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central motivation that adaptive time-stepping improves the accuracy/compute trade-off for neural solvers is not directly tested against a properly trained uniform-time-stepping neural baseline. The mean-Delta-t baseline is not sufficient because the neural solver is trained on variable Delta-t, making the mean step potentially out-of-distribution.

There is no empirical comparison to closely related adaptive/continuous-time neural PDE methods such as TANTE (Wu et al., 2025), Janny et al. (2024), or Hagnberger et al. (2024), despite their direct relevance. This makes the novelty and positioning difficult to assess.

The neural CFL model is trained only to imitate coarsened classical solver timesteps. It does not optimize timestep selection for neural-solver accuracy, stability, or computational cost, so the oracle comparison only shows closeness to a target Delta-t sequence, not that the sequence is optimal.

The proposed Euler and MoE timestep-conditioning strategies do not consistently outperform simple affine conditioning. Many differences are within error bars, and MoE adds substantial computational cost without conditional computation, so the claimed benefits of these components are not convincingly established.

Results are mixed across fields. In the coal dust explosion setting, gas y-velocity correlation is only about 20% and unrolled relative error is around 45%, yet the paper emphasizes an averaged correlation time of about 60%, hiding a significant failure on an important flow variable.

The evaluation is limited to three main 2D settings with small test sets (9-10 cases each) and fixed parameter ranges. There are no out-of-distribution or extrapolation tests, e.g., unseen Mach numbers, geometries, or shock strengths.

The paper does not quantify the practical benefit of adaptive stepping versus uniform neural rollout in the main text. A speed-accuracy comparison of adaptive versus uniform neural solvers with matched training data is missing.

Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete code/dataset availability statement (e.g., "code is publicly available as part of the library ." with no link or library name) and no clear indication that the generated datasets are released.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, claiming to be the first to learn temporal re-meshing with adaptable temporal resolution and concluding that ShockCast is "effective" is too broad given the mixed field-wise results and missing baselines.

Hypersonic results are unconvincing: a moderately sized MGN failed, only a subset of fields was modeled, and the paper relies on a special adapted U-Net. This limits the generality of the high-speed-flow claims.
The manuscript contains formatting and consistency issues, including an incomplete abstract sentence, table caption/content mismatches, garbled citations, and notation that is sometimes unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: adaptive temporal meshing for high-speed flows, where uniform time-stepping is impractical and shock-dominated dynamics require small local time scales.

Presents a clear and sensible two-phase framework, ShockCast, where a neural CFL model predicts the timestep size and a timestep-conditioned neural solver advances the flow state by that predicted step.

Introduces several physically motivated components for the neural CFL model, including spatial gradients, CFL-derived features, and max pooling, with ablations showing their utility in the more complex multiphase coal dust setting.

Develops novel timestep-conditioning strategies for neural solvers inspired by neural ODEs and Mixture of Experts, including Euler residuals and MoE-based conditioning, which are technically interesting and well-described.

Generates multiple new high-speed flow datasets (coal dust explosion, circular blast, spherical blast, airfoil shock, long circular blast, and hypersonic airfoil shock) with detailed CFD setup, potentially valuable for the community.

Evaluation is broad across several neural solver backbones (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver, MGN, DGN), conditioning strategies, and metrics (correlation time, TKE error, mean flow error, runtime, mass conservation).
Includes strong ablation studies comparing ShockCast against oracle Δt and mean-Δt baselines, which help isolate the effect of the learned timestep predictor.
Training details, hyperparameters, model sizes, and runtime analyses are reported, improving reproducibility relative to many neural PDE papers.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat limited relative to existing work on adaptive/continuous-time neural PDE solvers; the claim of being first to learn temporal re-meshing is overstated given prior timestep prediction, continuous-time interpolation, and time-conditioned multi-step models.

The paper cites related adaptive/timestep-learning methods such as TANTE, EAGLE, and conditional neural fields, but does not directly compare against them; the empirical comparison is largely internal to ShockCast variants plus oracle/mean baselines.

The proposed timestep-conditioning strategies show inconsistent and often marginal gains: affine conditioning is frequently best for correlation time, while Euler/MoE conditioning only helps on selected TKE or mean-flow metrics, so it is not clearly established when or why these mechanisms are preferable.

The neural CFL module is trained to regress coarsened ground-truth Δt values rather than to optimize an accuracy/compute trade-off or a learned adaptive policy, making the method feel closer to supervised timestep emulation than a fully adaptive solver.

Evaluation metrics may not fully capture high-speed flow quality: correlation time is dominated by smooth regions, and the paper lacks explicit shock-position/speed errors, phase errors, or detailed shock-capturing diagnostics.

Data and code availability is not clearly stated; the abstract sentence about availability appears garbled, and the generated datasets may be difficult to reproduce without a clear public release and documentation.
The theoretical motivation for adaptive time-stepping balancing the training objective and reducing variance is heuristic and not formally supported.

Some appendix results show substantial errors or instability for certain fields and conditioning variants, but the main text emphasizes the stronger settings, making the overall robustness of the approach less clear.
